analysis.one_liner: Exempts tribal businesses on Indian lands from federal labor-union law.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act, the federal law that gives most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively, so that any business owned and operated by an Indian tribe on tribal land would not count as an "employer" under that law. Workers at tribal casinos, hotels, and other tribal enterprises would lose access to the federal process for union elections and protection against unfair labor practices. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal governments and the businesses they own, especially casinos and hotels, would gain freedom from union-organizing drives and proceedings before the National Labor Relations Board. Tribes advancing this bill framed it as sovereignty: states and their subdivisions are already exempt from this labor law, and the bill would put federally recognized tribes in the same position.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds tribal enterprises on Indian lands to the National Labor Relations Act's list of bodies that are not considered "employers," removing them from the law's coverage.
The bill defines the covered entities broadly, reaching all lands within reservation boundaries, trust lands, and former reservation lands in Oklahoma.
Sponsors framed the bill as clarifying the rights of tribes on their own lands, aligning tribal governments with the existing exemption for state and local governments.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at tribal businesses, a workforce that includes many people who are not tribal members, would have no federal right to organize or bargain, and no federal forum to appeal to if they are punished for union activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers at tribal casinos and businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill places tribal enterprises outside the Act's definition of "employer," so its protections for organizing and collective bargaining would not reach their employees.
The bill text proposes no substitute federal or tribal forum protecting these workers' right to organize or shielding them from retaliation for union activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine argument on the sponsors' side: state and local governments are already exempt from the National Labor Relations Act, and tribes argue that applying the law to their enterprises treats sovereign governments like private companies. But as drafted, the bill settles that question by simply stripping the affected workers of federal union rights, with no replacement protection offered. The cost would fall on casino and other tribal-enterprise workers, many of them non-tribal members, while the benefit flows to the enterprises as employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Kline of Minnesota introduced the bill on March 9, 2009, joined by six original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On April 29, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 111th Congress.
Eight Republicans cosponsored the bill, and no Democrat did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, federal labor law coverage of tribal enterprises continued as it was, so tribal-enterprise workers and unions kept the status quo. The enterprises seeking the exemption gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. John Kline
for.role: Senior Republican, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: Rep. George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never held a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows only a referral to a subcommittee and nothing more.

sides.party_line_note: All of the bill's sponsors were Republicans (8 of 178 House Republicans cosponsored, plus its Republican sponsor), and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would exempt tribal casinos, hotels, and other tribally owned businesses from federal union law, freeing them from union-election petitions and National Labor Relations Board cases. The gain comes directly from the workforce, whose members would lose federal organizing and bargaining rights.
Unions would lose the ability to organize workers at tribal enterprises or bring unfair-labor-practice cases on their behalf, eliminating a growing pool of potential bargaining units.
